The ten thousand two hundred and third meeting of the Security Council is called to order. The provisional agenda for this meeting is the situation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian question. The agenda is adopted. In accordance with Rule 37 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite the following representatives to participate in this meeting: South Africa, Algeria, Australia, Austria, Brazil, Bulgaria, Canada, Cuba, Egypt, United Arab Emirates, Spain, India, Indonesia, Iraq, Ireland, Iceland, Japan, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Lebanon, Malaysia, Maldives, Morocco, Mexico, Namibia, Norway, Uganda, Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Qatar, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, Republic of Korea, Islamic Republic of Iran, Sri Lanka, Switzerland, Tunisia, Turkey and Vietnam. It is so decided. I propose that, in accordance with the provisional rules of procedure and the previous practice in this regard, the Council invite the permanent observer of the observer state of Palestine to the United Nations to participate in the meeting. There being no objection, it is so decided. In accordance with Rule 39 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite Mr. Ramiz Alakbarov, Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, to participate in this meeting. It is so decided. In accordance with Rule 39 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I also invite the following to participate in this meeting. His Excellency Mr. Kholi Sek, Chair of the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People. Mrs. Nasriya Elajja Fliti, Chargé d'affaires ad interim, Permanent Mission of the League of Arab States, and Mr. Quentin Weiler, Delegation of the European Union to the United Nations. It is so decided. The Security Council will now begin its consideration of item two of the agenda. I now give the floor to Mr. Ramiz Alakbarov.

Thank you very much. Mr. President, members of the Security Council, I am briefing you today as the situation in the West Bank is rapidly deteriorating, as we have witnessed in the last few days. This is compounding the already alarming conditions across the rest of the occupied Palestinian territory, with a wider escalation increasingly likely unless immediate steps are taken to reverse the course. Mr. President, let me also state at the beginning that the comprehensive plan to end the Gaza conflict and the Security Council Resolution 2803 must be implemented in full. This includes disarmament of Hamas and all armed groups, IDF withdrawal from Gaza, deployment of international stabilization force, and the transfer of governance responsibility to the National Committee for Administration of Gaza, NCA-G. Mr. President, earlier this month, I visited Gaza to assess humanitarian conditions and progress towards early recovery. The situation in Gaza has improved somewhat, but progress is far too slow. Recent weeks have seen some welcome progress in clearing solid waste from key areas and coordinating the entry of desperately needed sanitation equipment and supplies. I would like to recognize the facilitation of COGAT in this regard. These are positive steps, but they remain highly insufficient in the face of the immense needs on the ground. During my recent visit, I witnessed immense hardship amid continued displacement or crowded living conditions, widespread destruction, and nearly daily casualties caused by ongoing Israeli military operations. Yet, I also saw Palestinians in Gaza taking courageous steps against all odds to start rebuilding their lives. Health workers continue treating patients and rehabilitating clinics in extraordinarily difficult conditions. Community organizations are helping displaced families access shelter, education, and health services. and local actors are attempting to restore basic services in coordination with UN agencies and other humanitarian partners. At every stop of my visit, I met people determined to improve the lives of their families and communities. Their resilience is inspiring and provides a real glimmer of hope for what the future could hold. But I need to repeat my message to the Council that human dignity should not be conditional. The space for recovery so far has been denied. Community resilience cannot substitute the required supply of materials at scale, including those Israel considered dual use, or the political will to set Gaza on the path to a genuine recovery. As you have learned from the announcement earlier, the integrated phase classification report released last week showed improvements in food security and nutrition in Gaza. But the situation remains highly fragile and most families across the strip are still relying on humanitarian assistance as their only lifeline. With winter approaching, the window to provide an effective response to pressing shelter needs is closing fast. Mr. President, at the same time, the increase in Israeli airstrikes and the expansion of territory under Israeli military control continues to increase pressure on the population in Gaza. which is now confronted to around one third of Gaza. Gaza remains a dangerous place for UN to operate and deliver in, and I reiterate that under international humanitarian law, all parties must respect and protect civilians and humanitarian personnel, facilities and relief supplies, and refrain from actions that obstruct humanitarian operations. Mr. President, humanitarian assistance on its own cannot put Gaza on a sustainable track. As we work to increase the availability of aid, we must accelerate the transition to early recovery by restoring livelihoods, rehabilitating essential infrastructure, providing dignified shelter and supporting Palestinian institutions capable of leading recovery and reconstruction. The framework for doing so is clear and has been endorsed by this Council in resolution 2803. It must be implemented without any delay. This will require the parties to fulfil their commitments as well as enhance coordination between all stakeholders, including between the Palestinian Authority and NCAC. In this regard, I take note of the steps taken by the Israeli authorities on 26 July to enable the deployment of ISF to Gaza. These efforts must be guided by the political goal of reunifying the West Bank and Gaza under a single legitimate sovereign Palestinian government, ending unlawful occupation and restoring a political process towards a viable two-state solution. Israel's legitimate security concerns must be addressed. I'm encouraged by the ongoing meeting of the Global Alliance in Rome, as well as second convening of the Palestine donor group in Brussels on 15 July, in which I participated with UN colleagues. The meeting co-chaired by European Union and the PA demonstrated broad international consensus on the need for close coordination in the implementation of the resolution 2803. Mr. President, building a viable future for Gaza will not be possible if PA is pushed to the brink of collapse or if the current dangerous dynamics in the West Bank are left unchecked. In the past week, the escalating violence in the West Bank has resulted in civilian casualties, displacement, damage to property, and growing insecurity across affected communities. Israeli settler attacks against Palestinian communities, homes, places of worship, and civilian infrastructure have persisted at alarming levels. Attacks by Palestinians targeting Israelis have also resulted in civilian casualties as well as damage to property. On 23 July, two Palestinians, including a child, were killed in confrontations with Israeli settlers following a fire on agricultural land south-east of Nablus. The following day, violent incidents in Palestinian communities south-west of Nablus resulted in the killing of four Palestinians and two Israelis, injuries to several others, and extensive damage to Palestinian property. I urge Israel to take immediate and effective measures to prevent settler violence, protect Palestinian communities, and ensure that all perpetrators are held accountable. Palestinians must unequivocally reject violence and incitement and take all necessary measures to prevent attacks against Israelis. Israeli military operations, demolitions, and displacement of Palestinians also continued while Israeli authorities imposed further movement restrictions and accelerated settlement expansion efforts. On 14 July, Finance Minister Smotrich announced that Israeli Security Cabinet had allocated 1.3 billion shekels towards the placement of temporary housing units in dozens of new settlements throughout the West Bank prior to the approval of the formal Israeli plans for these settlements. He later announced the approval for the establishment of a new settlement in the northern West Bank, where Israel had previously evacuated settlers as part of the 2005 disengagement plan. I reiterate that all settlements are illegal under international law. I call upon all parties to take urgent steps to reverse the dangerous trajectory in the West Bank. I am deeply concerned by repeated unauthorized entry of Israeli forces and officials into the UNRWA Qalandia training center in East Jerusalem yesterday, while classes were in session. We are on premises and vulnerable and immune from any form of interference. Mr. President, the PA's fiscal situation remains critical as Israel continues to withhold Palestinian revenues. The PA is currently unable to deliver many critical public services, including education and health services, or pay full salaries to its civil personnel. Preserving viable corresponding banking arrangements is essential to maintain political Palestinian financial stability and economic activity. I welcome recent steps by Israeli authorities to facilitate the extension of these arrangements. However, Israeli correspondent banks have indicated the intent to terminate banking arrangements in the coming months. I urge continued engagement by all parties to avoid further deterioration, which could be disastrous. On July 9, Palestinian President Abbas issued a decree setting the date for the next Palestinian legislative elections across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem and Gaza, on 28 November. I welcome this announcement and reiterate that an inclusive and credible electoral process would represent an important step towards strengthening governance and responding to the aspirations of the Palestinian people. I encourage all stakeholders to work towards creating the conditions necessary for these elections to take place, including the participation of all eligible Palestinian voters. The UN stands ready to support Palestinian efforts in this regard in coordination with the Central Electoral Commission. Mr. President, this conflict continues to unfold amid wide regional tensions that impact levels of funding, the availability of supply lines, as well as security and political dimensions. Highlighting the urgent need for the deescalation and sustained effort to promote just and durable regional peace and stability, the trilateral framework within the US, State of Israel, and the Republic of Lebanon announced on the 26th June, constitute a milestone in efforts to end decades of conflict and then once lasting stability. I welcome the launch of the pilot zone operations and encourage Lebanon and Israel to fulfill their obligations and advance the full implementation of the Security Council resolution 1701. Mr. President, the determination and the selflessness I witnessed on my recent visit to Gaza must be matched by sustained and coordinated international engagement. There are positive signs of this commitment and mobilization at the recent gathering in Brussels. We must now carry this momentum forward. Resolution 2803 and its transitional arrangements must be implemented in full. Concurrently, the urgent steps might be taken to reverse the rapid deterioration in the West Bank, support the PA, and lay the groundwork for its return to governing Gaza. A coordinated approach is needed to ensure that these efforts are mutually reinforcing. Ultimately, Gaza's reconstruction cannot be sustained in the absence of political process Similarly, a political process cannot succeed while Gaza remains devastated, violence escalates in the West Bank, Palestinian institutions remain divided, and security conditions continue to deteriorate. And urge this Council to use its voice and effort to ensure that its resolutions are translated into meaningful actions on the ground. UN will continue to engage with all stakeholders and harness its operational capacity on the ground to advance this agenda and support the better future of Palestinians and Israelis. Thank you so much for your attention.
I thank Mr. Al-Akbarov for his briefing. I now give the floor to the permanent observer of the observer state of Palestine.

Mr. President, allow me at the outset to thank you for convening this open debate at this critical time. And let me thank Mr. Al-Akbarov for his briefing and his efforts. Mr. President, Palestinians continue being killed daily in bombardments in Gaza, in attacks by settlers and occupation forces in the West Bank. Killed as they sleep, as they tend to their groves, as they head to school, as they sit in their homes. Killed as if their lives never mattered, as if they were expendable. And they will continue being killed until those killing them are held accountable. Those who storm their towns, their villages, their homes, their lives, holding weapons and aiming it at them, want to hold our people responsible for the death that ensues, their death and the death of those attacking them who should not have been there in the first place. And as if that was not enough, The Israeli Prime Minister's conclusion is that the answer is more colonization, more disposition, more displacement, more violence. At a time where the situation in Gaza requires the full attention of the international community to stop the bloodshed and address the tremendous human suffering of our people and implement the resolutions of this council, as we have heard today, Israel is seeking escalation in the West Bank. Whether to justify further repression, to facilitate annexation and displacement, or for electoral purposes, yes, Confronted with the prospects of losing the upcoming election, Netanyahu is seeking electoral gains on the blood of Palestinians and even Israelis. This requires a strong international response before it is too late, as impunity is the reason for the persistence and escalation of these crimes. Mr. President, for years now, We have warned of settlers violence with the backing of Israeli occupation forces as an integral part of the Israeli strategy to annex maximum Palestinian land without, with minimum Palestinians. Some measures were taken, but in no way commensurate with the threat this terror represents against hundreds of Palestinian communities. The Israeli officials pay some lip service when the actions are too outrageous while continuing to create the conditions for their commission. Nothing was done by Israel to stop this violence. In the contrary, everything was done to fuel it. So it is the Israeli government that must be considered responsible for it, at par with the settlers committing it with the support of the Israeli occupation forces. For those trying to disseminate fake news and alternative realities, there are numerous videos online of settlers attacks across the West Bank. From those armed with automatic weapons to adolescents with sticks beating people, to those setting fire in houses and properties. There are videos of them doing all this while shouting insults and racist slurs and chanting death to Arabs, death to Arabs. The videos of the attacks by Israeli settlers at Tal village show them surrounding unarmed Palestinian civilians, holding them at gunpoint and threatening to shoot them. A Tal village is south of Nablus, as was, you know, indicated by Mr. Al-Akbarov. And too many times before that threat was followed, by actions to be taken lightly. The tales about hikers wandering around in the hills is ridiculous. The settlers came with one objective in mind, terrorizing the population to uproot it. One provocation after another, one murder after another. Our people are entitled to international protection. I repeat, Our people are entitled to international protection in the face of these repeated assaults, especially when asked not to respond to violence by violence, even as self-defense. When the occupying power, which is responsible for providing protection for the civilian population under occupation in accordance with international humanitarian law, The occupying power is abdicating its responsibility. Therefore, it is the responsibility of the international community to provide our people with protection. This Council and the General Assembly have adopted resolutions calling for such protection, but it is nowhere to be found. Israeli settlers must be disarmed, I repeat, must be disarmed. as this Council's resolution state to stop them from terrorizing our people. Action is needed. They need to be disarmed. And Israeli settlers and occupation forces have to leave our land and leave us alone. We don't want to see anyone killed. We want our people to live in freedom and dignity in their land. We want the occupation to end and peace to prevail. Mr. President, Jerusalem holds a diverse and rich history that was preserved over centuries thanks to the respect for the historic status quo. The images of Israeli extremist officials, soldiers, and settlers storming Al-Haram al-Sharif are the definition of provocation and incitement, fueling dangerous tensions. This is an integral part of the scorched earth policy, aiming to inflame tensions in the hope that the fire can be insurmountable and instrumentalized. A short-sighted and irresponsible approach. Mr. President, the resolutions of this council are unequivocal in opposing annexation and forcible displacement. So why are they still ongoing? There are upcoming elections in Palestine and in Israel. What signal will the international community send? We have on one hand, on one side, a Palestinian government committed to nonviolence and peace, and on the other side, an Israeli government unleashing brutal violence and committed to annexation. That question can only be resolved with strong international mobilization. To uphold international law and empower those seeking peace and restraining those who seek to destroy any such prospects. Let me repeat, to uphold international law and empower those seeking peace and restraining those who seek to to destroy any such prospect. There is nothing to wait for and everything to act for. to show we are not doomed to repeat history over and over again and that a different path is possible. The council has responsibilities. States have obligations. They can ensure the parties uphold theirs. That any upcoming government understands that Palestinian land is not for grab and Palestinian lives are not expendable and Palestinian rights have to be recognized and respected. That violence is a dead end, a cycle that will consume everything around it. That the time for peace is right now. No more delays or excuses. That no one is entitled to negotiate or destroy the other, to negate, sorry, or destroy the other. No one is entitled to negate or destroy the other. Many lives would have been saved had this been done a long time ago. Many lives hanging in the balance today. No more delays, no more excuses. Thank you very much, Mr. President.
I thank the permanent observer of the observer state of Palestine for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Israel.

Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank Mr. Abakarov for his briefing. It has been over eight months since this council passed resolution 2803. It established a path forward for Gaza. The Board of Peace was created. to set the stage for a new non-radical leadership. Countries have contributed to the international stabilization force. Aid is getting in at levels not seen since 2023. But while Israel upholds its end of the deal, the main problem remains Hamas has refused to disarm. But Hamas doesn't feel any pressure because the UN and this council refuse to call them out, to weaken them, to pressure them. I quote Mr. Mladenov, the High Representative for Gaza on the Board of Peace. I quote, every week without agreement is paid for by the population of Gaza, not by those refusing to agree to it. While this council has failed to pressure Hamas to accept the Board of Peace roadmap, The people of Gaza suffer. And not only that, this council still refuses to designate Hamas as a terrorist organization. This month we saw these problems in practice. The UN released a statement. It implied Hamas stormed a food distribution plant in Jabalia and that they assaulted two truck drivers at a World Food Program warehouse. The statement described, and I quote, an increasingly dangerous pattern of intimidation, violence, and obstruction. Good morning, United Nations. This is what we have been telling you for years, for years. But this statement, it was missing something. The statement mentions, quote, armed personnel. It mentions de facto authorities. It says this group is placing humanitarian workers at risk and disrupting the delivery of life-saving assistance. I looked very carefully. I searched paragraph by paragraph for the name of this group. I could not find it. This statement is missing Hamas. They are not mentioned even once. And I ask myself why? Why can't the UN call Hamas by name? Is the Secretary General telling you not to do that? Is the UN afraid? Afraid to say Hamas? Afraid of the governments that fund Hamas terrorism? This failure to call out terrorists by name and designate them must end now. For years, we talked about Hamas's efforts to sabotage, prevent, and block humanitarian aid. But instead of taking action, this council wastes its time repeating Hamas propaganda that Israel limits aid and starves civilians, that Israel closes border crossing, and that Israel does not comply with resolution 2803 and phase one of the 20-point plan. Just take a look at the new IPC report that examined the nutritional situation in Gaza. The report documents humanitarian improvements. Food insecurity is decreasing in every part of the strip. But Israel, we still have reservations about this report. The report unfortunately must repeat the Hamas propaganda. It must reach the same alarmist conclusions that there is food crisis in Gaza. The report claims that aid getting into Gaza is not enough. But that is not true. It is a lie. Because the projections are based on a flawed reporting process, incomplete sources of information, and anti-Israel bias. This month, an Israeli report showed the humanitarian situation in Gaza is stable. Over 600 trucks are entering Gaza per day. Not 100, like the IPC report says. Delivering over 1.8 million tons of food since the ceasefire began. This is above the World Food Program's benchmark of 80,000 tons per month. You know what? We can argue about which report is more accurate, but the most reliable indicator that food security is improving, food prices have decreased by over 70%. No one can argue with that. That means more families can access and purchase food at reasonable rates. The medical situation is improving as well. 18,000 tons of medicine and medical equipment have entered Gaza since the ceasefire began, and hospital capacity is up 50% since September. Israel is not just making progress on aid. On Sunday, the Israeli security cabinet approved the initial entry of the international stabilization force into Gaza. So we can start a pilot project for reconstruction in Rafah, creating a humanitarian zone without Hamas control. Mr. President, despite the complicated situation, Israel has been facilitating humanitarian assistance into Gaza. I'm sure that like every month, we will hear today remarks regarding the entrance of dual use items into Gaza. items that can be used for humanitarian purposes and for terrorist activities. We know what happens when these dual-use items get into Hamas's hands. Look at this picture. Hamas posted this video, you can find it online. It's a picture of the video. You can see Hamas terrorists digging up water pipes and turning them into rockets. And they actually put that video, that they're taking the water pipes and actually transforming them into rockets. Still, many members of this council call for Israel to let all of these items in without understanding the consequences or the reality on the ground. Our policy was not designed to make things harder for the people in Gaza. It is to prevent Hamas from rearming. We work with the UN, with NGOs to find alternatives, and we make exceptions when necessary. But as long as Hamas is in Gaza, there will be restrictions. Let's admit it. With Hamas in power, there is no future for Gaza. I now speak directly to Hamas. The ball is in your court. Either you disarm, either you give up power voluntarily, or Israel will do what is necessary. Mr. President, if we needed a reminder of Hamas's intentions, we were reminded this month. Hamas elected a new leader. Khalil Al-Haya as its next chairman. They elected one of the architects of October 7th as its new leader. He's an arch terrorist. Do you remember him? He was in Doha on October 7th, front and center on video with Ismail Haniyeh, the former chairman of Hamas. He watched the terrorists invade Israel and kill innocent civilians. He was proud of it. He celebrated it. He cheered them on. After he was elected, the vice president of the moderate Palestinian Authority called to congratulate him. And look what happened on Friday. A terrorist in Samaria killed two Israelis and injured three more. They murdered Benayahu Melet, a 32-year-old agriculture director, and they murdered Major Yuval Ezra. a 27-year-old IDF commander. Hamas not only praised the attack, they called for more violence. Mr. President, let us examine the irony in this council. Look at the list in front of you, at the countries that will speak today. Some of these countries are hosting Hamas as we speak, both their military and political leadership. They are facilitating their banking infrastructure, and they are giving them the oxygen they need to survive. Today, they will come here, will sit here, and they will call for a new future for Gaza. But at the same time, they embolden the terrorist organization that holds the people of Gaza hostage. So maybe you should ask them, When the representatives of Turkey will sit here later today, or Qatar, ask them if they allow Hamas banking to function in their countries, if they allow transfers to different banks in the world before they tell us what should happen in Gaza. Mr. President, while Israel is fighting terrorism at home, New York is becoming the latest battlefield. Last week, Mayor Mamdani accused our Prime Minister of being a war criminal and accused our nation of committing genocide. Hours later, a Jewish man walked out of his synagogue on the Upper West Side. He was stabbed by a radical who yelled, "Allah Akbar." When the mayor of New York City uses his microphone to demonize Israel, Terrorists with weapons get the message. Some attack with guns, some attack with screwdrivers, some attack with lies. It is all the same because it all leads to the same result, violence against Jews. Mr. President, Israel understands the challenges of a democracy fighting against terrorism. Israel knows what we have to do if Hamas will not disarm. The question is what will you do? This council should also take action. You should designate Hamas as a terrorist organization, and you should sanction Hamas so they cannot fund their crimes. This council should not be afraid to use those tools. But until now, this council has failed to fulfill its responsibilities. And not just with Hamas. You have not designated the Houthis. You have not designated Hezbollah. You have not designated the IRGC. Designate them now. You have the responsibility. You have the authority. Mr. President, to conclude, Israel has set a realistic path forward. We know what's going on in Gaza. Hamas is refusing to disarm. They are refusing to comply with the border of peace. and they are refusing to implement resolution 2803. Hamas continues to choose smuggling over aid, violence over progress, and terror over peace. But now Hamas has lost the chance to choose because they have shown the world that they don't want to change. Israel will ensure that Hamas will be disarmed. Israel will not wait forever. We understand that if we do not disarm Hamas, no one else will. It is our responsibility to ensure that Hamas can never again threaten the people of Israel. And we will fulfill that responsibility. Now this council has its work cut out for itself. It is time for action. Designate Hamas, sanction Hamas, and prevent Hamas terrorism once and for all. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Israel for the statement. I now give the floor to those Council members who wish to make statements. I give the floor to the representative of the United States.

Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to Deputy Special Coordinator Alec Bahrav for sharing your views. Colleagues, earlier this month, representatives from the Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the NCAG, met in Cyprus. We thank Cyprus for hosting this meeting, which showcased how our partners will continue to move ahead with President Trump's peace plan for Gaza, as endorsed in this Council's resolution 2803. The United States will continue to support the Board of Peace and the NCAG as they work toward a Gaza that offers prosperity, security, and dignity for all of the people in Gaza. The discussion in Cyprus included in-depth planning for the transition to the new NCAG-led governance structure in Gaza, which is urgently needed and will be possible as soon as Hamas decides to put down its arms, to which it committed when it agreed to the peace plan. We welcome the pledges from several European countries launching the Team Gaza initiative, a total of nearly $1 billion in early recovery money for Gaza. These projects must be carried out in close coordination with the NCAG and the Board of Peace. Uncoordinated efforts will undermine the NCAG's credibility and bolster Hamas. Detractors may say that it can't be done. But they are wrong. We know we will succeed, united by our confidence and determination to create a new future for the people of Gaza with the support of those who believe in the promise of Resolution 2803. Right now, three very different futures are possible. In one future, which becomes more likely if Hamas fails to disarm, war returns to Gaza. In another, the international community turns a blind eye, as it has done far too many times already. That would allow Hamas to hold the Palestinian people in Gaza hostage for years to come, threatening the security of Israel and the entire Middle East, and guaranteeing that a stunted, aid-dependent way of life remains the only option for people in Gaza. Neither of these futures is acceptable. With their commitment to action, our partners in the region and in Europe are opening the door on the third and transformative option. That door is the plan put forward by President Trump, implemented through the Board of Peace and the NCAG, permitting clear-eyed Palestinians from Gaza, determined to break the vicious cycle of the past, to move forward into the brightest possible future. Hamas has proven by its actions that it will do everything they can to retain power. They hope that we, the supporters of that bright future, the international community, will give up and turn a blind eye. I am here to say we will not. That is why the Board of Peace is moving forward with pilot programs in the areas it can, beginning in southern Gaza, despite Hamas's continued intransigence and refusal to put the people in Gaza first. We thank our Israeli partners for their assistance. in getting these pilot programs off the ground. These projects will move forward and will demonstrate that what all of Gaza can be as soon as Hamas decides to uphold their commitments to the peace plan. And we've seen other welcome developments in the past few days. Morocco officially signed up as a troop contributor to the International Stabilization Force on July 15th, the first country to do so. We applaud and congratulate Morocco for achieving that distinction. Others will soon follow suit, and the ISF will be prepared to provide security for the pilot projects and other areas as we move forward with implementation of the next phase of the peace plan. Another welcome development has been the unprecedented exposure of the truth about Hamas. On July 12th, the UN put out a statement that laid plain what we have known for years. Hamas continues to obstruct and exploit humanitarian operations in Gaza. They continually put the lives of aid workers in danger. They raided a World Food Program warehouse and assaulted the truck drivers there. As Dr. Al-Akmar Barov said in his statement, these incidents are not isolated. They are a pattern. And although this welcome acknowledgement of reality comes late in the game, as we say, better late than never. Colleagues, we all know the facts. Hamas has no place in Gaza. The people in Gaza know this. They have been intimidated into submission, but that won't last forever. We also know that UNRWA has no place in Gaza. We have been clear about that as well. Hamas cannot play any role in the future of Gaza because of what they stand for, not for the people in Gaza, but as a proxy for the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Iran's ties to Hamas are the reason Hamas will not disarm. Iran wants to keep the Palestinian people hostage to Hamas. We cannot and will not let them. Iran also wants to keep Hezbollah in business in Lebanon. We won't allow that either. Durable peace requires that sovereign governments, not terrorist proxies, exercise full control over their territory. The historic talks between the governments of Israel and Lebanon, enabled by President Trump's leadership, will continue to that goal. Building on the historic trilateral framework signed on June 26th, we look forward to continued negotiations as we look to restore peace and stability in the region. For decades, Iran kept the Syrian people under the thumb of the brutal Assad family. That is over now too. The United States will continue to support Syria's transition, including by working with the Syrian government to bolster its efforts to counter terrorism and drug trafficking, eliminate the remnants of chemical weapons, hold perpetrators of atrocities accountable, and secure investment and assistance for the benefit of the Syrian people. The United States is committed to lasting peace in Syria, both internally and with its neighbors. Special Presidential Envoy to Iraq and Syria Tom Barak continues to support engagement among groups within Syria and between Syria and Israel that could advance peace and stability throughout the entire region. And in Yemen, where the Yemeni people have suffered for far too long, the Houthis have once again demonstrated that they are doing little more than acting on behalf of Iran. The Houthis are attempting to hold the world hostage in the Bab al-Mandab, just as the IRGC has done for weeks now in the Strait of Hormuz. To meet the political and security challenges throughout the Middle East, we must recognize a simple truth. Throughout the region, many conflicts are fueled by a single actor, the Islamic Republic of Iran, with political and financial support from certain members of this council. The United States once again condemns in the strongest possible terms Iran's outrageous and unacceptable attacks against neighboring countries. This council must ensure that dialogue produces action. The United States remains committed to practical diplomacy that reduces conflicts, protects civilians, strengthens legitimate institutions, and advances a more stable and peaceful Middle East. We urge all UN member states to join us in working toward that goal. I thank you.
I thank the representative of the United States for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of France.

Thank you, President. President, I'd like to begin by thanking the Deputy Special Coordinator, Ramiz Alaghbarah, for his briefing. We have also listened very closely to the permanent observer of Palestine and the permanent representative of Israel and their important briefings. President, our debate cannot be separate from the reality of the region, because in the Middle East the sound of weapons still echoes, population displacement continues, and terrorism has not been contained. Civilian populations remain the primary victims of military escalation. The resumption of hostilities in the Gulf undermines the diplomatic progress achieved through the signing of the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran and threatens regional security. France condemns Iran's indiscriminate strikes against countries in the region and its attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Navigation through that maritime route must remain safe and free without restrictions or tolls. France is preparing to contribute to this effort with its partners through a neutral and strictly defensive multinational maritime escort mission. We call on the Houthis to immediately cease their destabilizing activities, which we strongly condemn. It is imperative that Iran fulfill its commitments under the Memorandum of Understanding and that negotiations resume in order to achieve a lasting resolution to the Iranian crisis, notably through a verifiable framework governing Iran's nuclear program. France stands ready to support all efforts in this regard. In Lebanon, France welcomes the tripartite agreement signed on June 26th, thanks to the engagement of the US as a first step towards implementing resolution 1701. The objective remains the restoration of the authority of the Lebanese state throughout its territory in full respect of its sovereignty and territorial integrity. We call on Hezbollah to surrender its weapons and permanently renounce its military activities. We call on Israel to withdraw fully from Lebanon. France reiterates its support for UNIFIL until the expiration of its mandate. Any future international engagement in Lebanon must meet the expectations of the Lebanese authorities and avoid any security vacuum in southern Lebanon. France and Italy are proposing an ad hoc international coalition to support the Lebanese armed forces and assist them in implementing their commitments. In Syria, The recent visit of the President of the Republic marked a new stage in our support for the political transition, including through the signing of a number of investment contracts aimed at rebuilding this country devastated by war and to engage in its reconstruction. We welcome the Secretary-General's recent visit to Damascus, which testifies to the growing mobilization of the international community. call on the international community to continue its efforts in this regard. And finally, President, let us not forget that the first anniversary of the New York Declaration on the two-state solution and the peace plan for Gaza is approaching. Nearly one year later, the situation remains worrying. It is urgent to implement resolution 2803, which requires the disarmament of Hamas. the removal of obstacles to humanitarian action and reconstruction, and compliance by Israel with its international obligations. In the West Bank, we condemn the acceleration of settlement activity, which is illegal under international law. The forthcoming launch of tenders for the E1 project poses a threat to the two-state solution. We are deeply concerned by the current violence in the West Bank. As the Israeli authorities have announced the launch of a major military operation, France calls on all parties to exercise calm and restraint and recalls the responsibility of the Israeli army to protect civilian populations. The increasing violence perpetrated by settlers against Palestinians is unacceptable, and France will continue to work with its European partners to sanction those responsible for settlement activity and settler violence. Nearly one year after the adoption of the New York Declaration, we must redouble our efforts to implement the two-state solution, which is the only viable solution for peace and the recognition and respect of the rights of the Palestinian people and Israel's rights to security. Mr. President, France will always stand alongside those who are committed to peace. It is the responsibility of all parties to return to the path of dialogue and and hostilities, and it is the responsibility of this Council to demonstrate collective determination in encouraging them to do so. Thank you.
I thank the representative of France for his statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Denmark.

Thank you, Mr. President, and I would also like to thank Special Representative Alok Bharav for his briefing. Mr. President, we convene today as countries across the Middle East stand on the brink of further escalation. Once again, Iran is attacking countries in the region and vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Denmark strongly condemns these actions, which threaten both regional stability and a key maritime shipping route. We remain committed to the stability of the region. We also strongly condemn the recent attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia, including on vessels in the Red Sea. These actions further undermine regional stability and threaten freedom of navigation. We stand in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region and reiterate our call for immediate and unconditional de escalation. In Lebanon, we urge all actors to adhere to the trilateral framework agreement and implement their commitments and call for respect for Lebanon's sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence in line with resolution 1701. Mr. President, while these crises demand our full collective attention, They do not diminish our responsibility elsewhere. As we've heard, the suffering in the occupied Palestinian territory has not paused, and nor should our resolve. The terrible violence over the weekend across the West Bank demonstrates just how volatile the situation has become. It comes on top of a series of concerning developments, reflecting a broader systemic trend of erosion of the two-state solution. This includes the Israeli authorities issuing tenders for the construction of illegal settlements in the E1 corridor, which threatens to separate East Jerusalem from the West Bank and divide the West Bank in two. It also includes rapid settlement expansion, expelling Palestinians, and eroding the social cohesion of Palestinian society. Meanwhile, settler violence continues to rise, accounting for 55% of all physical injuries in the West Bank. There are already more Palestinian fatalities linked to settler attacks in 2026 than in all of 2025. We also see deepening impunity as the IDF either fails to stop violent acts by settlers or actively takes sides of the settlers without holding perpetrators accountable. These developments are deplorable and these actions violate international law. We urge the Israeli authorities to take immediate measures to prevent further attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian communities and ensure the protections of civilians in the West Bank. We further urge the Israeli authorities to ensure effective law enforcement and accountability for perpetrators. Mr. President, in Gaza, the situation remains catastrophic. Civilians live in ever-shrinking territories. in improvised tents in inhumane conditions with insufficient access to nutritious food, clean water, and basic healthcare. The latest report from the IPC shows that more than half of Gaza's population still faces crisis levels of food insecurity or worse. Israel's restrictions on international NGOs operating in the occupied Palestinian territory further undermines stability and Palestinians' access to basic services. We call on Israel to allow full, immediate, safe, and unhindered access and sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance at scale into and throughout Gaza. Meanwhile, Israeli attacks continue, with over 1,000 Palestinians killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, including 294 children. 180 Palestinians were killed in July alone. This cannot continue. The only way forward is for all parties to strictly adhere to the ceasefire agreement. This includes disarmament of Hamas. Moreover, the international stabilization force and the Palestinian police force must be deployed without delay. Mr. President, the challenges facing the West Bank, including in East Jerusalem and Gaza, should not be addressed in isolation. They are key obstacles to the Palestinian people's legitimate aspiration to establish an independent, sovereign, and viable state under a reformed Palestinian leadership along the 1967 borders as part of a two-state solution, living side by side in peace and security with Israel. In closing, this renewed escalation across the Middle East and the Gulf, shows how fragile regional stability remains. At the same time, we must not lose focus from the suffering of the Palestinian people and the urgent need for a two-state solution. Denmark will continue to work for both, a stable Middle East and a credible path toward a two-state solution. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Denmark for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Somalia.

Mr. President, I thank Deputy Special Coordinator Al-Akbarov for his sobering briefing. We gather again as the Palestinian people endure deep suffering while the Middle East faces ongoing instability and a worrying disregard for international law. Eight months after the Security Council Resolution 2803 has been adopted, Its goal of ending conflict, expanding aid, and starting reconstruction remain largely unfulfilled, with little real progress for the civilians in Gaza. Somalia reiterates its call for the full implementation of Resolution 2803. Humanitarian aid is a legal duty, not a political tool. Civilians must receive assistance quickly, safely, and in the scale of their needs. All crossings should remain consistently open and restrictions on essential goods such as fuel, medicine, water, and supplies must be lifted. We recognize the value of humanitarian benchmarks for the monitoring of resolution 2803, but they must be verified by the United Nations and humanitarian actors throughout the reporting period. International humanitarian and human rights law must always be respected. Civilian humanitarian workers, civilian and humanitarian workers, and the UN staff must be protected. We support Somalia remains deeply concerned by the reports of torture, sexual violence, and missing Palestinians. We support establishing mechanism to account for missing persons and reunite families. Mr. President, Gaza's health system crisis is alarming. Thousands, including children and cancer patients, need urgent evacuation as essential medicines run out and hospitals ration care. The medical corridor to the West Bank must be restored, but the evacuation cannot substitute for rebuilding Gaza's health system. Destruction of water, sanitation, and electricity infrastructure has created public health emergency. Without basic services, civilians are trapped in crisis regardless of market availability. Israel, as the occupying power, has the responsibility to allow basic services, including health services, and evacuate patients the right to return. Somalia rejects any attempt to fragment Gaza or prevent safe, voluntary return of displaced Palestinians. We condemn the continued expansion of military-controlled areas in Gaza, which restrict movement, block family returns, and raise fears of permanent displacement. Gaza's recovery and unification of governance must be Palestinian-led and supported by the region and international community, anchored to a two-state solution. We reiterate that Gaza is an integral part of the occupied Palestinian territory and a future Palestinian state. Mr. President, while Gaza draws global attention, the West Bank, as we heard, including East Jerusalem, also face dangerous deterioration. Somalia remains gravely concerned about the continued illegal settlements, settler terrorism, forced displacement, land confiscation, arbitrary detention, and destruction of Palestinian properties. These actions violate international law and Security Council resolutions and must cease immediately. In recent days, Mr. President, I have also seen one of the largest incursions of Al-Aqsa Mosque, with more than 4,000 Israeli settlers and far-right groups entering the compound under heavy police protection while Palestinian worshippers were barred entry. We unequivocally condemn the occupying power's actions, which represents a dangerous escalation and a violation of the historic and legal status. of this holy site. We emphasize that Jerusalem status cannot be changed by unilateral actions. The historical and legal status quo at the holy sites must be respected by Israel, and all incitements of violence must stop immediately and unconditionally. Mr. President, Somalia welcomes the renewed momentum behind the two-state solution including efforts by Saudi Arabia, France, and the New York Declaration. Concrete actions, not just statements, are needed to preserve the foundation of a future Palestinian state, including the release of the Palestinian Authority's tax revenues withheld by Israel. Humanitarian aid cannot substitute for a political solution, and reconstruction cannot succeed amid occupation and settlement expansion. Somalia stands firmly for an independent, sovereign Palestinian state along the pre-1967 borders with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital. Turning to Lebanon, Somalia is concerned by the tensions along the Blue Line. We call for the full implementation of Resolution 1701, respect for Lebanon's sovereignty and international law. We take note of the ongoing strategic review of post-UNIFIL presence and stress the importance of maintaining a strong and meaningful UN presence to deter further escalation and support stability in Lebanon and beyond. In Syria, Somalia supports the Syrian-led political process per resolution 2254. We condemn Israeli military incursions inside Syria and call for Israel to fully withdraw from all Syrian territories in line with its obligation under relevant United Nations Security Council resolution and the 1974 disengagement agreement. In Yemen, Somalia calls for respect for its sovereignty and support for the Yemeni-led, Yemeni-owned political process under UN auspices. Mr. President, recent escalations in the Gulf show how fast conflict can spread in the Middle East. Somalia urges restraint, diplomacy, and respect for the sovereignty of all states and international law. Equally important is to guarantee freedom of navigation in the international waterways, including the Strait of Hormuz, and to refrain from actions that undermine maritime security and the free flow of global commerce. To conclude, Mr. President, regional security must rest on mutual respect, good neighborliness, and peaceful coexistence in accordance with the UN Charter. To achieve this in the Middle East is essential to address the common denominator and the root cause of the elusive peace in the Middle East. There can be no peace in the Middle East without addressing the long-standing occupation and annexation of Arab lands, including the Palestinian state. We remain committed to working with all Council members to that end. I thank you, Mr.

President.
I thank the representative of Somalia for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Panama.

Thank you, Mr. President. Panama is grateful for the convening of this quarterly open debate and for the briefings that we heard from Mr. Ramiz Alagbarov, and we thank him also for his constant efforts. We welcome the representatives of the delegations who honour us today with their participation. For too long now, the peoples of the Middle East have witnessed one crisis after another. without any definitive resolution of the root causes of the conflicts. Although some situations do show encouraging signs of easing and openness to dialogue, others continue to be marked by violence, displacement and a humanitarian crisis that continues to affect millions of people. In Gaza, Nine months of an albeit shaky ceasefire have partially alleviated some of the most urgent needs for the population to the extent that it is worth also recognising that humanitarian assistance has increased. Nonetheless, the cumulative consequences of the conflict are plain to see in the daily lives of thousands of families, while tremendous challenges remain to rebuild hospitals, schools, homes, water systems and other essential services that were destroyed during the war. Panama reiterates the need for humanitarian assistance, which fortunately has been flowing better, we reiterate the need for this to continue to arrive in full, safely and unhindered, at the required scale, on a sustained basis and without disruption by extremist parties. It is also important to preserve the necessary conditions for UN agencies and humanitarian organisations to carry out their work safely, independently and with full respect for international law. What is happening in Gaza can also not be uncoupled from the West Bank. The expansion of settlements, demolitions, the displacement of communities and measures that progressively change the territorial reality continue to erode the necessary conditions to preserve a credible political horizon. Gaza and the West Bank form part of a same political and territorial reality. Accordingly, any path towards peace should address them comprehensively, preserving their territorial continuity, strengthening a reformed Palestinian Authority, and avoiding unilateral measures that continue to dispel the possibility for a negotiated solution enabling Israelis and Palestinians to live in peace, security and dignity. President, in Lebanon, the intensification of hostilities seen since March has had a profound humanitarian impact, with thousands of people killed and wounded, as well as more than one million displaced. Although the relative de-escalation seen since the end of June is an encouraging sign, the persistent military activities, violations of the airspace and restrictions on UNIFIL's freedom of movement prove that the situation on the ground remains fragile. Panama is hopeful and optimistic regarding the progress made in the recent conversations between Lebanon and Israel facilitated via United States mediation. efforts to ensure that this process can consolidate the cessation of hostilities, advance in implementing the agreements reached and give rise to the necessary conditions for a lasting peace. Panama reiterates its commitment to the sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity of Lebanon within its internationally recognised borders. Panama likewise reaffirms its support for the work of UNIFIL to support stability along the Blue Line. We strongly condemn attacks on UN personnel and we reiterate that all parties must guarantee their security, respect the inviolability of the UN's premises and ensure full freedom of movement for the mission. In addition, We believe that the discussions regarding the future presence of the United Nations in Lebanon should respond to the current reality on the ground, avoiding creating security vacuums and ensuring that any mechanism agreed by this Council enjoys the necessary capacities to be able to implement its mandate effectively. Syria is facing a different challenge. The recent political progress provides an opportunity to strengthen the state's institutions and broaden the participation of different sectors of society, provided that this new phase is supported by concrete measures in transitional justice, the rule of law, national reconciliation and clarifying the fate of missing persons. Terrorism continues to pose a serious threat to the transition and to the country's stability. Panama condemns the attacks aimed at undermining the political process. We reiterate the need to avoid any action that heightens tensions, fully respecting the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of Syria. In the meantime, the prolonged and dangerous tensions relating to the Strait of Hormuz and Iran demonstrate that military confrontation does not constitute the path towards a solution. Indeed, a solution can only be achieved through political dialogue, good faith negotiations and delivery on the commitments agreed. Panama supports diplomatic efforts to promote de escalation, to keep communication channels open and to prevent tensions building into a broader confrontation. Attacks and threats on merchant vessels, including Panamanian flagged vessels in the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and other maritime routes in the region that we strongly condemn, imperil those vessels' crews, affect international trade, and compromise the security of global supply chains. Mr. President, every fresh escalation in the region ends up fueling another crisis. Every lost opportunity for dialogue protracts the suffering of millions of people. The United Nations continues to play an irreplaceable role. The work of the Secretary General and his special envoys, peace operations and humanitarian agencies is keeping spaces for dialogue open, supporting political processes and providing assistance to those most in need. The peoples of the Middle East deserve a future defined by peace and dignity. Panama will continue to support any initiative aimed at transforming dialogue into agreement, agreements into trust, and trust into a lasting peace for the region. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Panama for that statement. I now give the floor To the representative of Greece.

Thank you, Mr. President. And let me thank Deputy Special Coordinator Alakbarov for his remarks. Recent developments in the Middle East remind us how fragile regional stability remains and how quickly tensions can escalate. From Gaza to Lebanon, Syria, and the Gulf, the challenges before us are interconnected. Respect for international law, including the UN Charter, and determined diplomacy must guide our collective response. The United Nations has an indispensable role to play. This means safeguarding freedom of navigation and ensuring unimpeded transit through international straits, including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, in accordance with international law, as reflected in UNCLOS. We will continue cooperating closely with our international partners, including France, the United Kingdom, and Saudi Arabia, to promote initiatives defensive in nature that safeguard freedom of navigation and maritime security. Greece stands in solidarity with its regional partners and strongly condemns illegal and unprovoked attacks against civilian infrastructure and international shipping by Iran. We equally condemn continued threats and attacks by the Houthis against maritime shipping to and from Saudi Arabia. Greece will strengthen its cooperation with Saudi Arabia and the GCC member states in promoting regional stability and prosperity. Our commitment to the global non-proliferation architecture remains unwavering. The NPT and the IAEA remain its indispensable pillars. Iran must therefore commit clearly and unconditionally to an exclusively peaceful nuclear policy. Mr. President, turning to Lebanon, we welcome the framework agreement and the subsequent direct talks in Rome between Israel and Lebanon facilitated by the United States. The direct Israeli-Lebanese track offers a genuine opportunity to advance towards sustainable peace and it deserves our full support. The path to lasting stability lies in the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 1701, the restoration of the Lebanese state's authority throughout its territory and the disarmament of all non-state armed groups so as to ensure the state's monopoly on the legitimate use of force. We stand firmly behind President Aoun and the Lebanese government as they undertake this daunting task. Greece remains Greece maintains a strong engagement with Lebanon across the military, economic and diplomatic fields. We will continue supporting the Lebanese armed forces, both bilaterally and together with our partners. Greece has also provided funding to Lebanese hospitals and we will continue assessing projects aimed at addressing Lebanon's socio economic needs and supporting a sustainable path towards prosperity for all Lebanese. We are actively assessing the post UNIFIL period. An international presence will be required to ensure that the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon and the strengthening of the deployment of the Lebanese armed forces, particularly in the south, take place smoothly and in coordinated manner. Having been a significant contributor to UNIFIL from the outset, Greece stands ready to contribute and participate actively to discussions on the post-UNIFIL mission, including in the Security Council. In Syria, Mr. President, as discussed in this setting a few days ago, political transition with accountability, justice, and genuine national reconciliation is possible, and the newly formed People's Assembly could be an important step in this path. Translating commitments into actions will now ensure that all Syrians feel fully protected and represented. Greece intends to remain an active partner in this effort and supports deeper engagement between Syria and the United Nations, and we also welcome the historic visit of the Secretary General in Damascus. Mr. President, The need for a credible political horizon in Gaza remains as pressing as ever. The comprehensive peace plan for Gaza endorsed through resolution 2803 has created an opening which we should turn into lasting progress. Disarmament of Hamas is a priority and we commend the efforts of High Representative Mladenov In this regard, and we look forward to the deployment of the ISF in the strip. Addressing Israel's legitimate security concerns remains indispensable for building a durable peace. At the same time, the gap between humanitarian needs and the assistance reaching civilians in Gaza is alarming. Humanitarian actors, including UNRWA, remain indispensable. The Palestine Donors Group meeting in Brussels reaffirmed the international commitment to Gaza's recovery, including through the Horizon Fund. Greece will participate in the Team Gaza initiative launched by the European Commission. As a first step, we will focus on enhancing social and economic infrastructure across the strip. Transitional arrangements should reinforce, not replace, Palestinian institutions. We support the National Committee on the Administration of Gaza and the deployment of the newly vetted Palestinian police forces. Our collective objective is to support the Palestinian Authority in implementing reforms, paving the way for its return to Gaza, as provided for in Resolution 2803. In the West Bank, settlement expansion, forced displacement, demolitions, and settler violence against Palestinians, including Christian communities, violate international law and undermine the prospects for a negotiated peace. Preserving the status quo of the holy sites in Jerusalem is also essential for interfaith coexistence and regional stability. We call for the release of withheld Palestinian tax revenues and welcome the Palestinian Authority's reform efforts under exceptionally difficult circumstances. Greece will continue supporting these efforts, including through the European Union PEGAS mechanism channeling its funding to East Jerusalem hospitals. Mr. President, international initiatives such as the New York Declaration, demonstrate that support for peace remains strong. That support must be matched with a credible political process leading to the two-state solution. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Greece for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Liberia.

Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. We join in thanking the Deputy Special Coordinator and Resident Coordinator at the Office of the United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process. And we welcome distinguished colleagues to the chamber. Excellencies, every war, however protracted, eventually confronts a moment of strategic truth. The moment when the cost of continuing war far exceeds any conceivable gain from prolonging it. This is true of every protracted conflict, including this one. The briefing of today And the figures presented by ORCHA and other UN agencies confirm that the occupied Palestinian territory is approaching that point. We are no longer merely observing a crisis. We are witnessing the systemic erosion of the conditions necessary for human life itself. According to ORCHA, In the West Bank, fatalities from settler attacks this year have already surpassed the total for all of 2025. In Kalkilya alone, recent demolitions claimed homes, water networks, and 19 donor-funded settlers shelters, displacing dozens of families, including 34 children. In Gaza, the humanitarian catastrophe strikes at the very generation to come. Nearly 4,000 miscarriages were recorded in just the first six months of this year. Over 57% of pregnant women suffer from severe anemia. Beneath 60 million tons of rubble, human hope is being buried. The clearing of 630,000 tons of debris is not a sign of recovery. It is a drop in an ocean of ruin. This council must also not lose sight of the fact that the attacks of October 7, 2023 killed close to 1,200 people and took 251 hostages into Gaza, taking a toll on Israeli families. It took more than two years until January of this year before the last of them, living and deceased, were finally accounted for and returned home. That suffering is also a part of this record as well, and it must inform how the Council thinks about deterrence, justice, and the conditions for a lasting peace. Excellencies, Liberia speaks as a nation that walked through the fire of civil conflict. We speak from a continent that understands a fundamental truth: no society ever truly emerges from war simply because one side managed to exhaust the other. Peace does not begin when the last weapon fires. Peace begins when leaders find the courage to acknowledge that dialogue yields what weapons never can and never will. Liberia unequivocally condemns every attack against civilians by any party, anywhere, and at any time. We affirm without reservation Israel's legitimate right to live in peace and security, free from terror and the threat of future attacks. And we affirm with equal conviction the inalienable right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, freedom, and statehood. These rights are not mutually exclusive. They are mutually dependent. Security that denies dignity and humanity is an illusion. Dignity without security cannot endure. Lasting peace demands both. We therefore call upon this Council and all parties to act to guarantee full respect for international humanitarian law, to ensure unhindered aid access, to halt settlement expansion, forced displacement, and civilian destruction, to ensure full accountability and transparency in the treatment of all captives and detainees, and to urgently reignite a credible political pathway toward a durable and just two-state solution. Mr. President, to conclude, The greatest illusion in any protracted conflict is the belief that tomorrow's battlefield will produce what yesterday's battlefield could not. Peace is never achieved when one people surrender their future to another. It never will happen. Peace begins when both peoples finally reclaim their right to dignity and shared humanity. That is the responsibility of the parties. It is the solemn duty of this Council. And I thank you for your kind attention.
I thank the representative of Liberia for his statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of the Russian Federation.

Mr. President, we thank UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Remzi Alagbarah, for his briefing. The situation in the Middle East has been one of the main items on the Security Council's agenda since practically the very establishment of the United Nations. Nonetheless, despite decades of painstaking work, it is clear that the goal of achieving peace and prosperity for the countries and peoples of the Middle East remains far from being achieved. To our profound regret, it sometimes appears as though any diplomatic successes that we have witnessed, including in recent months, are simply erased every time. And the situation itself, rather than changing for the better, often continues to deteriorate, spreading to new territories and affecting nearly every country in the region without exception. New outbreaks of violence continue, the geography of the conflict expands, and as always, the greatest burden falls upon civilians. Although the deep-seated problems of the region are often overshadowed by the daily stream of news, we are convinced that the international community must not lessen its attention to an issue that remains fundamentally important for the Middle East, namely the Palestinian question. We regret that the implementation of the ceasefire agreements between Israel and Hamas in Gaza reached in October 2025 has largely stalled. Reports continue to emerge regularly of new operations by the Israeli Defense Forces resulting in continued civilian death and suffering. Restrictions persist on the import and delivery of humanitarian assistance. Donald Trump plan, which formed the basis of the peace agreements, remains on paper. The Board of Peace has essentially yet to become operational. The international stabilization force has still not been established. The prospects of a complete withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza remain dim. It is also clear that there are currently no practical actions being taken to launch reconstruction efforts in the Gaza Strip. U.S. peace efforts on the Palestinian track have effectively been currently put on pause. Despite efforts by the High Representative of the Board of Peace to Gaza, Nikolai Mladlanov, to secure agreement on the roadmap he has prepared together with mediators, it has so far proved impossible for the parties to reach mutually acceptable solutions. main stumbling block continues to be the difficult issue of demilitarizing the Palestinian enclave. Moreover, the document also lacks guarantees regarding the end of Gaza's occupation, let alone prospects for its political reunification with the West Bank and a long-term settlement of the Palestinian issue. The situation in the West Bank itself is also developing along a negative trajectory. Israeli authorities continue to strengthen their administrative and legal control over the territory. The pace and the scale of settlement expansion have long surpassed all records. We are concerned by reports received in recent days of unprecedented tightening of restrictions on the movement of Palestinians between different localities. As a result, irreversible realities are being created in the West Bank and the territories under Palestinian control continue to shrink. We have carefully reviewed the letter circulated ahead of today's debate from President of the State of Palestine Mahmoud Abbas, in which Deep concern is expressed over the escalation of violence in the occupied Palestinian territories, primarily in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. We believe that the expansion of settlement activity, along with attacks on Palestinians and the destruction of their civilian infrastructure, undermines the prospects for implementing this two-state solution and creates a risk of further deterioration of the situation. Russia is convinced that only a comprehensive settlement of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict on the basis of a well-established international legal framework can guarantee lasting peace and stability for all the peoples of the region. Opportunities to achieve this still exist, and we strongly urge all parties concerned to make use of them. Mr. President, the Ongoing negative trends in the context of the Palestinian-Israeli conflict are taking place against a backdrop of rising tensions in the Middle East overall. From this perspective, we're equally concerned by developments in and around Lebanon. In recent weeks, we have observed some positive momentum on the political and diplomatic track. This includes the launch, for the first time in more than three decades, of direct Lebanese-Israeli negotiations. under U.S. mediation, as well as the conclusion of the trilateral framework agreement on June 26. We also note the visit of Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to Washington last week. At the same time, negotiations have not resulted in a complete cessation of hostilities. Israel continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon, particularly north of the Litani River. According to reports, between July 25th and 27th, the IDF continued demolitions and controlled explosions of buildings in a number of Lebanese towns. The actions of the Israeli military pose a direct threat not only to the health and the lives of civilians, but also to those of UN peacekeepers, hindering the UN Interim Force in Lebanon from carrying out its mandate. Against this backdrop, Legitimate questions arise as to the potentially explosive consequences of winding down the mission in 2027 amid expanding Israeli occupation and the likely emergence of a security vacuum. We remain convinced that a complete cessation of hostilities and a political settlement of the Lebanese conflict remain imperative, including for the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 1701. President, We would be remiss not to recall that the latest escalation in Lebanon was a direct consequence of the aggression launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28th. Despite the signing of the Islamabad memorandum, made possible through the energetic and effective mediation efforts of Pakistan, Qatar, and several other regional states, the situation in the Persian Gulf not only remains extremely tense, but it continues to deteriorate. In recent weeks, we have witnessed another exchange of strikes that once again placed civilian infrastructure in Iran and in Arab states at risk. Risks have also emerged to navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, threatening serious consequences for global energy and food security. Our country has consistently called for a political and diplomatic resolution of the US Iranian conflict that takes the interests of all states in the region into account. Similar approaches apply to the situation in Yemen. The chronic unresolved crisis in that country, now in its second decade, undermines regional stability and creates risks of uncontrolled escalation on the Arabian Peninsula. Recent events in and around Yemen have unfortunately confirmed this assessment. We are convinced that the path to peace and stability in this Arab country lies through direct and frank dialogue among its main political forces, including the Ansar Allah movement. We consider antagonizing this movement to be counterproductive as it has long become an integral part of the country's military and political landscape. What is needed is renewed momentum in the UN-led mediation efforts overseen by the Secretary-General's special envoy, Hans Greenberg, with the participation of a broad range of Yemen's neighbors, including Saudi Arabia and Iran. Madam President, to conclude, We would like to note that the only way to achieve peace, stability, and prosperity in the region is diplomacy, negotiations, and building good neighborly relations among all the countries of the region while strengthening their security. A useful starting point could be narrower formats such as those envisioned in Russia's updated concept for collective security in the Persian Gulf. This document contains practical proposals for strengthening confidence-building measures and envisages a gradual approach to overcoming regional crises, ultimately leading to a stable and conflict-free Middle East open to broad international cooperation. Russia stands ready to engage in such cooperation and discussions with all interested parties regarding these and other constructive proposals aimed at ensuring a reliable and sustainable security architecture throughout the entire Middle East. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of the Russian Federation for that statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you, Madam President, and I also thank Deputy Special Coordinator Alakbarov for his briefing. Madam President, last November, this Council adopted UN Security Council Resolution 2803, endorsing President Trump's comprehensive peace plan for Gaza. It continues to offer a historic opportunity to achieve lasting peace, but eight months on, implementation risks stalling. Now is the time for all parties to fulfil their commitments under the plan in full. In that context, I will highlight three points. First, we need further action to improve the humanitarian situation in Gaza. Civilians continue to endure horrendous conditions, surrounded by sewage and rubble. We welcome the progress that has pulled Gaza back from the levels of famine seen last year. However, according to the IPC's latest snapshot, 1.2 million people still face significant food shortages, with projections indicating 90% of the population will remain dependent on humanitarian aid to survive. While food may be available in some private markets, it remains unaffordable or inaccessible for many Palestinians, particularly the most vulnerable. Averting famine cannot be a benchmark for success, nor can improving the humanitarian situation be conditional on progress on other tracks. Israel must fulfill its commitments under the comprehensive plan by ensuring unimpeded humanitarian access. This includes opening more crossings into Gaza, streamlining the dual-use approvals process, and allowing lifesaving and essential recovery items to enter. We are also deeply concerned by reports of Hamas obstructing humanitarian operations, as Deputy Special Coordinator Al-Akbarov set out today. That includes the recent incident at a World Food Programme distribution center. Actions that disrupt lifesaving assistance are unacceptable. The UN, including UNRWA and NGOs, must be able to operate safely and at scale so that they can help alleviate the suffering. Second, we need greater momentum on security, governance, and recovery in Gaza. We reiterate that Hamas must fulfill its commitments, decommission its weapons, and dismantle its terrorist infrastructure. This should be phased and verified alongside a strengthened Palestinian security presence, deployment of an international stabilization force, and a sequenced Israeli withdrawal. At the recent Palestinian donor group, the UK joined the Team Gaza initiative and announced over $13 million for the UN Horizon Fund. These commitments should support Palestinian-led delivery across all of Gaza.
